topic.name: GERD & PUD
objectives: Diagnose GERD clinically vs when to scope
H. pylori testing and eradication treatment
Red flag symptoms needing urgent referral

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Maria, 45, has had 'heartburn' for 3 years. She buys OTC antacids weekly. Recently she noticed food getting stuck in her chest when swallowing—she has to drink water to push it down. She lost 8 lbs without trying. Maria has classic GERD that's progressed to dysphagia—a RED FLAG that demands EGD to rule out Barrett's esophagus or esophageal cancer. 20% of US adults have GERD symptoms weekly. You'll see this every single day in primary care.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Diagram showing lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxed/open with stomach acid splashing up into esophagus, contrasted with a competent closed LES

content_chunks.title: What is GERD?
content_chunks.content:
**GERD** = chronic retrograde flow of gastric contents causing **troublesome symptoms** or **mucosal damage**.

**Pathophysiology**: The **lower esophageal sphincter (LES)** is weak or inappropriately relaxes. Other contributors: hiatal hernia, delayed gastric emptying, obesity, pregnancy.

**Classic Symptoms**:
• **Heartburn** (retrosternal burning, worse after meals, lying down)
• **Regurgitation** (acid or food comes up to throat)
• **Water brash** (excessive salivation due to acid stimulation)

**Atypical Symptoms** (easy to miss!):
• **Chronic cough** (second most common cause after post-nasal drip)
• **Globus sensation** (lump in throat)
• **Hoarseness** (morning worse)
• **Asthma-like wheezing**
• **Non-cardiac chest pain** (must rule out heart first!)

**Montreal Classification**: GERD diagnosed if mild symptoms ≥2×/week OR moderate-severe symptoms ≥1×/week
content_chunks.visual_desc: Anatomy diagram: esophagus, LES (weak/relaxed arrow), stomach, with acid reflux shown splashing into lower esophagus

content_chunks.title: 🔴 ALARM SYMPTOMS — Require EGD Before Starting PPI!
content_chunks.content:
**'Dysphagia, Odynophagia, Weight loss, GI bleeding'** — memorize this cold!

**Alarm (Red Flag) Symptoms requiring EGD**:
• **Dysphagia** (trouble swallowing — food sticks)
• **Odynophagia** (painful swallowing)
• **Unintentional weight loss**
• **GI bleeding** (hematemesis, melena, hematochezia)
• **Iron deficiency anemia**
• **Persistent vomiting**
• **Family history** of esophageal or gastric cancer
• **Age >60** with new-onset dyspepsia

**Why?** To rule out **Barrett's esophagus** (pre-cancerous intestinal metaplasia) and **esophageal adenocarcinoma**. Risk of Barrett's: 10-15% of chronic GERD patients. Risk of adenocarcinoma: 0.5% per year in Barrett's.

quick_checks.q: Which patient needs EGD before starting PPI?
quick_checks.explanation: Alarm symptoms (dysphagia + weight loss) require EGD to rule out Barrett's/esophageal cancer before starting symptom management.

quick_checks.q: Which is an ATYPICAL GERD symptom?
quick_checks.explanation: Chronic cough, hoarseness, globus, and asthma-like wheezing are atypical presentations. Classic symptoms are heartburn and regurgitation.

lessons.title: 💊 GERD Treatment: Putting Out the Fire

content_chunks.title: Lifestyle First (Works Better Than You Think)
content_chunks.content:
**These measures can eliminate the need for daily PPI in MILD GERD**:

1. **Elevate head of bed 6-8 inches** (use blocks, not extra pillows!)
   • Pillows only increase abdominal pressure → WORSE reflux

2. **Avoid lying down within 3 hours of eating**
   • Gravity is your friend!

3. **Weight loss** if BMI >25
   • Each 5 kg/m² increase = 2× risk of GERD symptoms

4. **Avoid trigger foods**:
   • Fatty/greasy foods (delay gastric emptying)
   • Chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, peppermint (LOWER LES pressure)
   • Spicy foods, citrus, tomato sauce (irritate esophagus directly)
   • Carbonated beverages (distend stomach → reflux)

5. **Smaller, more frequent meals** (don't stretch the stomach)

6. **Stop smoking** (nicotine relaxes the LES)

**How effective?** Weight loss + head-of-bed elevation + dietary changes = comparable to PPI in mild intermittent GERD!
content_chunks.visual_desc: Side-by-side: LEFT (wrong): patient lying flat after big meal with acid reaching upper esophagus. RIGHT (correct): bed head elevated with blocks, patient upright after meal, small portions

content_chunks.title: PPIs: The Heavy Hitters (Know This Cold)
content_chunks.content:
**PPIs** are first-line for moderate-severe GERD. They're the MOST potent acid suppressants.

**Mechanism**: Irreversibly block H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells → profound acid suppression.

**Examples & Dosing**:
• **Omeprazole** (Prilosec) 20 mg daily
• **Pantoprazole** (Protonix) 40 mg daily
• **Esomeprazole** (Nexium) 40 mg daily
• **Lansoprazole** (Prevacid) 30 mg daily
• **Dexlansoprazole** (Dexilant) 60 mg daily — dual delayed release

**⏰ CRITICAL Dosing Rules**:
• **Take 30-60 min BEFORE breakfast** (on empty stomach!)
• PPIs work best when taken before a meal — food activates the pumps, and PPIs need active pumps to work
• If once daily doesn't control symptoms → add SECOND dose before dinner (don't double the AM dose!)

**Duration of therapy**:
• GERD: 8-12 week course, then try to step down or stop
• Erosive esophagitis: 8-12 week course (may need maintenance)
• Barrett's esophagus: indefinite (protects against progression)

**Safety concerns (don't overuse PPIs!)**:
• Long-term use (≥1 year) → ↑ risk of:
  - C. diff infection (2-3× higher risk!)
  - Pneumonia (community-acquired)
  - Osteoporosis/fractures (hip, wrist, spine)
  - Vitamin B12 deficiency (impaired absorption)
  - Hypomagnesemia
  - CKD (possible association)
  - Gastric fundic gland polyps (benign but annoying)
• **Best practice**: Use lowest effective dose, try to stop after 8-12 weeks, or step down to H2RA as needed!
content_chunks.visual_desc: Clock diagram: 6:30 AM = take PPI, 7:00 AM = eat breakfast (pumps activate, PPI blocks them), 7:30 PM = if needed, second dose before dinner

content_chunks.title: H2RAs & Antacids: The Alternatives
content_chunks.content:
**H2 Receptor Antagonists** (H2RAs):
• **Mechanism**: Block histamine at parietal cell → ↓ acid production (less potent than PPIs)
• **Examples**: famotidine (Pepcid) 20 mg BID, nizatidine, cimetidine (rarely used — CYP interactions)
• **Best for**: Mild GERD, breakthrough symptoms on PPI, nighttime breakthrough
• **Key difference**: Faster onset than PPIs but less acid suppression. Tolerance develops in 2-6 weeks!
• **Pearl**: Add famotidine 20-40 mg at bedtime for nighttime reflux breakthrough in patients already on AM PPI

**Antacids**:
• **Examples**: Tums (calcium carbonate), Maalox/Mylanta (aluminum/magnesium)
• **Use**: Immediate PRN relief only (don't heal esophagitis)
• **Quick**: Onset in 2-5 minutes, lasts 1-2 hours
• **Pearl**: Great for mild intermittent symptoms, but if using >2×/week → patient needs step-up therapy

**Treatment Ladder**:
Mild intermittent → Antacids PRN
Mild persistent → H2RA PRN or scheduled
Moderate-severe → PPI daily × 8-12 weeks
Severe/erosive → PPI BID × 12 weeks → EGD to confirm healing

mnemonics.mnemonic: **AM-PPI = Before Breakfast**: take PPI **30-60 min before the FIRST meal of the day** (usually breakfast)
**GO-TO-PPI**: **G**oals (mild = antacid, ongoing = H2RA, **T**reatment = PPI, **O**ptimal = step down when better)

quick_checks.q: When should you instruct a patient to take their omeprazole?
a: With the largest meal of the day
quick_checks.explanation: PPIs must be taken 30-60 min BEFORE breakfast on an empty stomach. Food activates proton pumps, and PPIs need active pumps to work.

quick_checks.q: Patient with moderate GERD has completed 10 weeks of PPI with good control. Best next step?
a: Try to step down or stop
quick_checks.explanation: Best practice: use lowest effective dose for shortest duration. After 8-12 weeks, try step-down (lower dose, then H2RA, then PRN) or stop.

lessons.title: 🦠 PUD & H. pylori: The Ulcer Duo

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: James, 52, comes in with gnawing epigastric pain that wakes him at 2 AM. Eating makes it feel better for about an hour, then it comes back. He takes ibuprofen daily for 'achy joints.' His stool is dark and tarry. James has a classic **duodenal ulcer** caused by NSAIDs + possible H. pylori. He's now bleeding — this is a medical emergency. Peptic ulcer disease affects 4 million Americans yearly. H. pylori causes 80% of gastric ulcers and 90% of duodenal ulcers. This is a treatable, curable infectious disease — and you can prevent cancer!
content_chunks.visual_desc: Endoscopic view: ulcer crater in duodenal wall with visible inflammation, contrasted with normal healthy duodenal mucosa

content_chunks.title: Gastric vs. Duodenal Ulcers (Boards LOVE This)
content_chunks.content:
**Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD)** = break in the gastric or duodenal mucosa ≥5 mm with visible depth.

**Causes (the two big ones)**:
1. **H. pylori infection** (60-80% of ulcers — treatable!)
2. **NSAIDs** (20-30% of ulcers — preventable!)
3. Rare: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma), Crohn's, stress

**Gastric Ulcer vs. Duodenal Ulcer — KEY DIFFERENCES**:

| Feature | Gastric Ulcer | Duodenal Ulcer |
|---------|---------------|----------------|
| **Pain timing** | Worse WITH eating (30-60 min after) | Worse on EMPTY stomach, relieved by food |
| **Pain pattern** | 'Food makes it hurt' | 'Food makes it better' (2-5 AM pain) |
| **Location** | Lesser curvature of stomach | Duodenal bulb (first part) |
| **Cancer risk** | YES (needs biopsy at EGD!) | NO (never malignant) |
| **H. pylori link** | 60-80% | 90% |
| **Age** | Older (50-70) | Younger (30-60) |

**Key Point**: Gastric ulcers need ENDOSCOPY WITH BIOPSY to rule out malignancy. Duodenal ulcers almost never malignant.

**Complications**: **Bleeding** (most common — melena, hematemesis), **Perforation** (acute abdomen, board-like rigidity — surgical emergency!), **Gastric outlet obstruction**.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Split diagram: LEFT — stomach with gastric ulcer on lesser curvature, food entering. RIGHT — duodenal bulb with ulcer, pancreatic secretions flowing

content_chunks.title: H. pylori — Test and Treat!
content_chunks.content:
**Who to test?**
• Active PUD (found on EGD) — TEST EVERYONE!
• History of PUD (if not previously treated)
• **MALT lymphoma** (gastric — eradication cures 60-80%!)
• Early gastric cancer (post-resection)
• Dyspepsia with alarm symptoms → scope + biopsy
• Uninvestigated dyspepsia in high-risk populations?

**Best testing methods**:
| Test | Sensitivity | Specificity | Best for |
|------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| **Urea breath test** | 95% | 95% | Confirms active infection, confirms eradication |
| **Stool antigen** | 94% | 97% | Active infection test, good for eradication check |
| **EGD with biopsy** | Gold standard | — | Needed for diagnosis of PUD + can test histology |
| **Serology (blood IgG)** | 85% | 79% | ❌ CANNOT confirm active vs. past infection. Don't use! |

**⚠️ Rule**: Stop PPI for 2 weeks before testing (false negatives!). Also stop bismuth and antibiotics for 4 weeks.

**First-line Eradication Therapy** (local resistance permitting):

**Triple Therapy** (7-14 days):
• **PPI** BID (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg BID)
• **Amoxicillin** 1 gram BID
• **Clarithromycin** 500 mg BID

**Quadruple Therapy** (if clarithromycin resistance suspected or prior treatment failure):
• **PPI** BID
• **Bismuth subsalicylate** 524 mg QID
• **Metronidazole** 500 mg TID-QID
• **Tetracycline** 500 mg QID

**Confirm eradication**: Urea breath test or stool antigen 4+ weeks AFTER completing therapy (off PPI too!).

**If first-line fails**: Switch to quadruple therapy or refer to GI.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Treatment algorithm: Diagnose PUD → Test for H. pylori → If positive: Triple therapy (PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin) × 14 days → Confirm eradication 4 weeks later → If still positive: Quadruple therapy

content_chunks.title: PUD Management & Prevention Checklist
content_chunks.content:
**Active PUD Treatment**:
✅ PPI daily × 8-12 weeks (heals most duodenal ulcers in 4-6 weeks, gastric in 8-12 weeks)
✅ H. pylori eradication if positive
✅ STOP NSAIDs! Switch to acetaminophen if possible
✅ If NSAIDs needed: use COX-2 selective (celecoxib) + PPI co-therapy

**Prevention (High-Risk Patients on NSAIDs)**:
🔴 **Who needs GI protection with NSAIDs?**
• Age >65
• History of PUD or GI bleeding
• On anticoagulants or antiplatelets (warfarin, DOACs, aspirin, clopidogrel)
• On corticosteroids
• High-dose or multiple NSAIDs
✅ **Co-prescribe PPI** (omeprazole 20 mg daily) for any above risks

**When to refer/ER (RIGHT NOW)**:
• **Active GI bleed**: hematemesis, melena, hematochezia + hypotension/tachycardia
• **Perforation**: sudden severe epigastric pain, board-like rigid abdomen, free air under diaphragm on X-ray
• **Gastric outlet obstruction**: projectile vomiting, early satiety, weight loss
• **Failed H. pylori eradication** after 2 courses → GI referral
• **Gastric ulcer with atypical appearance** → needs EGD with biopsy

**Patient education**:
• Take NSAIDs with food
• Report black/tarry stools immediately
• Complete the full H. pylori treatment (7-14 days) even if symptoms resolve!

mnemonics.trigger: Gastric vs duodenal ulcer pain timing
mnemonics.mnemonic: **Duodenal = D**istal = **D**inner time (empty, wakes at night, food helps). **Gastric = G**reater curve = eating **G**rieves (pain after meals)

quick_checks.q: A patient's epigastric pain is relieved by eating but returns 2-3 hours later and wakes them at night. Most likely diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: Duodenal ulcer pain: empty stomach = pain, food = relief, nighttime awakening is classic. Gastric ulcer = pain WITH eating.

quick_checks.q: Which H. pylori test should you NOT use to confirm eradication after treatment?
quick_checks.explanation: Serology tests IgG antibodies — cannot distinguish active from past infection. A positive result could be from a prior treated infection. Use breath test or stool antigen at 4+ weeks post-treatment.
